To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Ca2+ buffering properties in vulnerable hypoglassal motoneurons in mutant SOD1 transgenc mice are not significantly altered as compared to nontransgenic animals.
Ca2+ buffering properties in motoneurons are differentially regulated between ALS-resistant and ALS-vulnerable neurons, and that this difference is not affected by expression of mutant (G93a) SOD1.
Ca2+ buffering is low in hypoglossus motoneurons of ALS transgenic mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a better understanding of the pathomechanism and pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases.
a quantitative analysis of the Ca(2+) homeostasis of hypoglossal neurons of mutant SOD (G93A).
the identification of cellular risk factors in ALS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
low Ca2(+)-buffering in motoneurons is not sufficient to induce degeneration but may be necessary.
the low Ca2+ binding capacity in motoneurons is a prerequisite but not a sufficient factor for degeneration.
the vulnerability of motoneurons in ALS is not due to an increased Ca2+ buffering capacity per se, but to a combination of factors, including a low Ca2+ binding capacity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ALS is a Ca2+ dependent disease, which is characterized by a selective vulnerability of motoneurons, which are characterized by an intrinsic low Ca2+ binding capacity.
the vulnerability of motoneurons is due to a pre-existing, genetically determined Ca(2+)-sensitivity
low Ca2+-binding in ALS-resistant neurons is a prerequisite for resistance, and that low Ca2 +-binding in vulnerable neurons is an important risk factor for degenerative processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the vulnerability of motoneurons to Ca2+-induced death can be explained by their low Ca2+ binding ratio.
a low Ca2+ binding ratio may represent a general risk factor for degenerative processes in motoneurons.
ALS-related degeneration of motoneurons is not due to a general defect in Ca2+ homeodynamics, but is rather associated with a specific vulnerability of motoneurons to Ca2+ overloading.
